## Why this unit matters

- Epidemic data arrive in discrete intervals; many simulations advance in fixed
  steps.
- Two flavours of discrete-time SIR:
  - a **deterministic function map** (continuous state);
  - a **stochastic Markov chain** (integer counts).
- As $\delta t\to0$ the map converges to the continuous ODE — tying discrete and
  continuous worlds together.

## Equations {.smaller}

Per-step probabilities (@eq-s-ch02-probs) from the SIR rates; the map moves
expectations, the chain draws binomials:

$$
p_I = 1-e^{-\beta c I_t \delta t/N},\quad p_R = 1-e^{-\gamma\delta t}.
$$ {#eq-s-ch02-probs}

$$
\text{map:}\;\; S_{t+1}=S_t-p_I S_t,\;\; I_{t+1}=I_t+p_I S_t-p_R I_t,\;\; R_{t+1}=R_t+p_R I_t.
$$ {#eq-s-ch02-map}

$$
\text{chain:}\;\; Y_t\sim\text{Bin}(S_t,p_I),\;\; Z_t\sim\text{Bin}(I_t,p_R).
$$ {#eq-s-ch02-chain}

The map is the chain's one-step conditional expectation.

## Julia API: two kernels side by side

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch02-kernels
#| echo: true
using Distributions, StableRNGs
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function map_step(state, p, δt)                     # deterministic
    S, I, R = state
    inf = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    rec = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    (S - inf, I + inf - rec, R + rec)
end
function chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)              # stochastic
    S, I, R = state
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)
end
function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, n; extra = ())
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, n + 1); traj[:, 1] .= u0; s = Tuple(float.(u0))
    for k in 1:n; s = step(s, p, δt, extra...); traj[:, k+1] .= s; end
    traj
end
```

## Generated result: map vs chain

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-ch02-compare
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Infectious compartment: stochastic chain realisations (grey), their mean (red), and the deterministic map (dashed). The map tracks the stochastic mean."
using CairoMakie
u0 = [990, 10, 0]; δt = 1.0; n = 40; ts = 0:n
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
mapt = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, n)
nsims = 200
ens = [iterate_model(chain_step, u0, p, δt, n; extra = (StableRNG(seed),)) for seed in 1:nsims]
chainI = reduce(hcat, (t[2, :] for t in ens)); meanI = vec(sum(chainI; dims = 2)) ./ nsims
fig = Figure(size = (760, 380)); ax = Axis(fig[1,1]; xlabel = "day", ylabel = "I(t)")
for j in 1:nsims; lines!(ax, ts, chainI[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.1)); end
lines!(ax, ts, meanI; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "chain mean")
lines!(ax, ts, mapt[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 3, label = "map")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt); fig
```

## Validation: convergence to the ODE

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch02-check
#| echo: true
using OrdinaryDiffEq
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end
ref = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, float.(u0), (0.0, 40.0), p), Tsit5();
            reltol = 1e-12, abstol = 1e-12, save_everystep = false).u[end]
δts = [40.0 / 2^k for k in 5:12]
errs = map(δts) do dt
    m = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, dt, round(Int, 40.0 / dt))
    maximum(abs.(m[:, end] .- ref))
end
order = sum(log2(errs[k] / errs[k+1]) for k in 1:length(errs)-1) / (length(errs) - 1)
cons = all(k -> isapprox(sum(mapt[:, k]), 1000.0; atol = 1e-8), 1:n+1)
(round(order; digits = 3), isapprox(order, 1.0; atol = 0.1), cons)
```

First-order convergence and conservation confirmed.

## Limitations & takeaways

- The **chain** is most faithful: integer counts, chance extinction, run-to-run
  variability shrinking *relative to* population size.
- The **map** is its cheap, smooth mean-field shadow — blind to fluctuations.
- As $\delta t\to0$ the map tends to the **ODE**, the chain to the
  **continuous-time Markov chain**: different limits.
- A within-step artefact (no infect *and* recover in one step) vanishes as the
  step shrinks.
- **Takeaway:** discrete models bridge data cadence and continuous theory.

::: {.notes}
Stress that the map is the chain's expectation for one step from a given state,
which is why the red mean and dashed map run so close together. They are not the
same curve: the update is nonlinear, so iterating the expectation is not the same
as averaging the chain, and the map's peak sits above the ensemble mean. The convergence study measures
first-order behaviour: halve the step and the error halves. The calculus
prerequisite derives the same result for forward Euler and is optional
background. Encourage learners
to shrink δt in the notebook and watch both the discretisation error and the
extinction probability change.
:::
